source.title: IDInit: A Universal and Stable Initialization Method for Neural Network Training
source.authors: Yu Pan; Chao-Zheng Wang; Zekai Wu; Qi-Fan Wang; Min Zhang; Zeng-Lin Xu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table formatting is flattened, so individual values in Table 1 cannot be reliably assigned to methods.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether initialization choices affect training convergence and trainability across network types and depths, using accuracy, loss, and epochs-to-threshold rather than training classification error.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results about initialization and convergence that bear on V3 and V4. Table 1's flattened values are not assigned to rows because the method-to-value mapping is unclear. The paper does not report training classification error or test the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: The AllConv experiment directly compares initialization-dependent trainability in a plain convolutional network, bearing on V4. The unusual long-residual-stem experiment also tests the stability of normalization-free Fixup training, bearing on the Fixup clauses of V3 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that IDInit improves convergence, stability, and performance across their tested settings. They argue that SGD breaks identity-initialization symmetry and momentum strengthens this effect. Their symmetry analysis does not itself establish a general convergence-rate guarantee, and they acknowledge that the improvement mechanism remains unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces IDInit, an identity-based initialization with padded identity-like matrices, patch-maintain convolution, and small values to address dead neurons. It does not reproduce the claim's named initialization studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization choice, optimizer, learning rate and weight decay, warm-up, network type and depth, and IDInit components are varied or discussed as affecting outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual CNNs, ViT, BERT, and GPT-Base-MOE show initialization-dependent convergence improvements.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Identity-based initialization can accelerate optimization in residual CNNs and Transformers under the tested training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: Initialization ablations and comparisons improve endpoint classification accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization choices can improve final classification accuracy under a fixed training budget.

record.problems: Most reported classification results are accuracy rather than training error. Some findings are figure-based, and the paper does not give exact numerical values for the AllConv or Res-112 training outcomes in the prose. Table 1 formatting is too flattened to map its numbers to methods.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 in Section 4.1 was left out because its flattened layout does not reliably associate the displayed values with individual methods and conditions. Figure-only details not stated in prose, including exact AllConv and Res-112 accuracy values and intermediate curve readings, were not transcribed.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error, random or corrupted labels, CIFAR-100, and model-size or regularization effects.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious-local-minimum frequencies, and extra student neurons.

Depth-dependent training-error degradation in plain batch-normalized CNNs, matched shortcut controls, longer training, and very deep plain tanh training. The Fixup result concerns one unusual 109-layer residual stem.
Greater trainable depth under a depth sweep, very deep tanh networks, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and 10,000-layer convolutional training. AllConv provides evidence at one depth only.
Initial linearized stability thresholds, catapult dynamics, curvature evolution, edge-of-stability behavior, and divergence relative to those thresholds.
Matched batch-normalization versus no-normalization comparisons of accuracy gain, training speed, and learning-rate tolerance; whether Fixup matches normalized networks' speed.

record.verdict_notes: Verdicts use only the supplied text. Residual-network improvements are not treated as direct tests of V4's explicitly plain-network claim. R16 should become separate initialization-specific rows. Table 1 and omitted figure readings were already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: No training classification error results; no random or corrupted-label benchmark comparison.
No two-layer teacher-student experiment or spurious-local-minimum rate.

Does not compare plain and shortcut networks at increasing depth. Tests a long residual-stem network without batch normalization using IDInit, Kaiming, and Fixup; does not test plain tanh networks or Fixup without normalization.
Does not test the cited Glorot, He, Schoenholz, Pennington, or Xiao methods directly, nor compare orthogonal with Gaussian weights.
No learning-rate stability-limit or edge-of-stability experiment.
No batch-normalization versus no-normalization speed or learning-rate-tolerance comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet-20
rows.operation_detail: Train with IDInit and both proposed modifications for 200 epochs.
rows.baseline: 87.01±0.29 (direct identity matrix; no IDICτ or IDIZCε)
rows.note: This is test accuracy, not training error. The paper reports four ablation settings; rows R1–R3 retain the individual settings it explicitly describes.
rows.check: Endpoint test accuracy in a residual network does not establish V4's faster learning or greater trainable depth in plain networks. Weight decay is internally inconsistent: Section 4.2 gives 5e-5, Appendix B.3 gives 5e-4.

rows.subject: ResNet-20
rows.operation_detail: Train with IDInit without IDICτ or IDIZCε.
rows.note: Ablation comparator; the paper describes this as the lowest accuracy among the four settings.
rows.check: A single endpoint test accuracy does not measure an incomplete initialization effect on training speed or trainable depth.

rows.subject: ResNet-20

rows.note: The paper reports this setting improves accuracy by nearly 5.89% over setting (i).
rows.check: This residual-network ablation measures endpoint test accuracy, not V4's plain-network training speed or trainable depth.

rows.subject: ResNet-20

rows.note: The paper reports this setting improves accuracy by nearly 3.42% over setting (i).
rows.check: This residual-network ablation measures endpoint test accuracy, not V4's plain-network training speed or trainable depth.

rows.subject: AllConv
rows.operation_detail: Train with IDInit; compare with Kaiming and IDInit without IDICτ.
rows.baseline: Without warm-up, Kaiming and IDInit without IDICε fail to train.
rows.value: IDInit can train AllConv and maintains the highest performance in all situations.
rows.locator: Appendix C.2, Figure 16 and accompanying text
rows.note: The text names IDICτ in the setup and IDICε in the result. No exact numerical values are stated in the accompanying prose.
rows.check: Remove V3: there is no depth sweep, shortcut comparison, or very deep plain tanh experiment. For V4, retain the explicit no-warm-up trainability comparison. The result's IDICε notation conflicts with the setup's IDICτ; IDIZC is explicitly unused.

rows.subject: Res-112
rows.size_stated: 112 layers; 109 layers in the residual stem
rows.operation_detail: Train without batch normalization; compare IDInit, Kaiming, and Fixup.
rows.baseline: Kaiming and Fixup fail to train after 4 epochs.
rows.value: IDInit successfully trains this network and the standard derivation of the output converges to a stable value.
rows.locator: Appendix C.6, Figure 19 and accompanying text
rows.note: Figure 19 contains accuracy and output standard-deviation curves, but the prose supplies no exact accuracy values.
rows.check: Split by initialization. Fixup's claimed stable normalization-free training is absent: its outputs explode and training fails after four epochs. IDInit succeeds, but that does not support the Fixup-specific clauses. Remove V4 because this is a residual network.

rows.check: The loss and Jacobian comparison concerns a residual network. It does not test V4's plain-network claim or compare normalization conditions for V6.
